name: Cetilistat

lead: Cetilistat is a pill that blocks fat-digesting enzymes so some of the fat you eat passes out of the body instead of being absorbed. The aim is fewer calories absorbed and a leaner look.

It inhibits pancreatic and gastrointestinal lipases, so triglycerides are not broken down. Phase 2 trials reported weight loss in obese patients and, in people with type 2 diabetes, weight and HbA1c reductions, with tolerability described as comparable to or better than orlistat.

paras: It is taken as a pill with meals and used alongside a calorie-conscious diet. It was developed by Alizyme, Takeda and Norgine and is reportedly approved in Japan, with limited availability elsewhere.
Side effects are digestive, such as oily stools, urgency and flatulence, and absorption of fat-soluble vitamins may be reduced. It is not widely available.

angle.text: Cetilistat blocks intestinal fat digestion so fewer calories are absorbed, leading to weight loss and a leaner look. Phase 2 trials reported weight loss, and it is available mainly in Japan.

lead: Cetilistat (ATL-962) is a pancreatic lipase inhibitor developed as an anti-obesity drug. Like orlistat, it blocks intestinal enzymes that break down dietary fat, so some ingested fat is excreted rather than absorbed.[1][2]
It completed Phase 1 and 2 trials in Western countries and was developed in Japan with Takeda, which reportedly obtained approval to market it there. Takeda ended its license with Norgine in 2018.[1]

Phase 2 trials reported weight loss in obese patients and, in people with type 2 diabetes, weight and HbA1c reductions with tolerability described as comparable to or better than orlistat.[3][4] It does not have broad international availability.

Pancreatic lipase breaks down roughly half or more of dietary triglyceride in the gut, which is why blocking it changes how much fat reaches the bloodstream.[5] Cetilistat belongs to this class and has been described in reviews as a candidate alongside orlistat.[4][6]
infobox: Marketed in Japan per Wikipedia; not broadly approved elsewhere

paras: In looksmaxxing and weight-management discussions, fat blockers are mentioned as a way to lower the calories absorbed from a meal and so support a leaner physique alongside diet and training. Cetilistat appears in these conversations mainly as a lesser-known relative of orlistat that is not marketed in most countries, so it is discussed far less than orlistat itself.

Its developed indication is obesity, including obesity with type 2 diabetes, where trials tracked body weight and HbA1c.[4][7] Reviews of new anti-obesity drugs have listed it among agents with a prospect of approval and noted that adverse events with these drugs were rather rare and tended to decrease with treatment duration.[8]

Cetilistat is a benzoxazinone derivative, chemically 2-(hexadecyloxy)-6-methyl-4H-3,1-benzoxazin-4-one, with a long sixteen-carbon ether chain attached to the ring and the molecular formula C25H39NO3 (molar mass about 401.6 g/mol). It is also known by its development code ATL-962.[1] The long lipid-like chain suits a molecule that works in the fatty environment of the gut, and a rat study reported that cetilistat inhibited human pancreatic lipase roughly nine times more potently than it inhibited rat lipase.[9]

Orlistat, the reference drug in this class, was approved by the US FDA as Xenical in April 1999, became available over the counter as the half-strength Alli in June 2007, and was cleared for non-prescription sale in the EU in January 2009; it is reported to block absorption of roughly 30 percent of dietary fat.[10] Pooled trial data summarised by Wikipedia show about 2 to 3 kg more weight loss than control over a year when combined with diet and exercise.[10]

Cetilistat works through the same mechanism. In the 2007 twelve-week placebo-controlled trial, weight loss was reported as similar to what is seen with orlistat, with side effects also similar, and in the 2010 trial in obese people with type 2 diabetes cetilistat was reported to reduce weight and HbA1c and to be better tolerated than orlistat.[1][3][4] The practical difference most discussed in the literature is tolerability, since oily stools and urgency are the main reason people stop lipase inhibitors; for orlistat, Wikipedia notes that these effects are strongest at the start and tend to lessen over time, and that limiting fat to about 15 g per meal reduces oily stools and flatulence.[10]

The appearance goal is a lower body-fat percentage, visible as a leaner waist, face and jawline. Lipase inhibitors contribute indirectly: fat that is not absorbed is not stored, so total calories absorbed fall when meals contain fat, and in trials this is measured as body-weight change.[3][4] Researchers note that the drugs act on absorption only and do not change appetite, so reviews place them as one option alongside diet, exercise and other medications.[2][11]
After the drug is stopped, regain is documented for the class: Wikipedia reports that up to 35 percent of lost weight was regained after orlistat treatment ended.[10]

A phase II, multicentre, randomized, placebo-controlled 12-week study of 442 obese patients (371 randomized after a hypocaloric diet run-in) examined cetilistat's efficacy, safety and tolerability.[3] A 12-week trial in obese patients with type 2 diabetes on metformin compared cetilistat at three doses with orlistat and placebo; the primary endpoint was body weight change, and secondary endpoints included other obesity measures.[4] Wikipedia summarises the 2007 study as showing weight loss similar to orlistat, and the 2010 trial as showing significant weight reduction, HbA1c reduction and better tolerability than orlistat.[1]

Registered phase 1 and 2 trials (NCT00148382, NCT00156897) examined fat excretion and efficacy in obese diabetics.[7][12] Reviews of obesity drugs in development have described cetilistat among the lipase inhibitors beyond orlistat.[11][13] A study in rats reported reduced body weight gain and improved lipid profiles.[9]

In the 12-week obese-diabetic trial, participants were randomized to placebo, one of three cetilistat doses taken three times daily with meals, or orlistat, after a two-week run-in; the primary endpoint was absolute body-weight change.[4] The registered phase 2 trial of this design enrolled about 600 people, and the phase 1 fat-excretion study about 80.[7][12]

Reported effects mirror orlistat: oily or loose stools, fecal incontinence, frequent bowel movements and flatulence. Because fat-soluble vitamin absorption may also be reduced, supplementation may be needed to prevent deficiencies.[1]
Cetilistat inhibits gastrointestinal lipases, preventing hydrolysis of dietary triglycerides, so unabsorbed fat is excreted.[1][3]

Pancreatic lipase hydrolyses dietary triacylglycerol into absorbable free fatty acids; inhibiting it leaves triglyceride intact and it passes through the gut.[5] In a rat study, cetilistat inhibited human pancreatic lipase roughly nine times more potently than the rat enzyme, with an IC50 of about 6 nmol/l for the human enzyme.[9] A randomized study in healthy volunteers measured reduced dietary fat absorption with cetilistat compared with orlistat.[14] The drug acts in the gut lumen rather than through the brain, which distinguishes it from appetite-suppressing obesity drugs.[11]
Alizyme developed the drug and went into administration; Norgine BV then acquired the global rights. By 2009 it was in Phase 3 trials in Japan with Takeda.[1]
A 2020 screening study of approved drugs identified cetilistat as having anti-SARS-CoV-2 activity in vitro.[15] This is unrelated to its weight-loss use.

Cetilistat has been marketed in Japan according to Wikipedia, and has not received broad approval elsewhere, so people outside Japan cannot ordinarily obtain it through standard prescribing.[1] Orlistat, its comparator, is the lipase inhibitor available over the counter and by prescription in many countries.
